extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, and critics interested in language, literary style, poetry, drama, and the effects of democratic social conditions on literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles and stylistic criteria for language, poetry, and drama as affected by democratic social conditions; useful for judging or producing literary works in or about democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear phraseology / avoid semantic ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Without clear phraseology there is no good language; giving unwonted meanings to existing expressions often renders a word indeterminate and leaves writers pointing at a knot of ideas rather than a single thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: successive writers twisting an expression in different ways so that its meaning becomes ambiguous. Examples: authors doubling meanings of words leads readers to be unsure which sense is intended. Scoring note: clarity of a term's meaning and stability of usage are valued above novelty that creates ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid careless neologisms from partisan/technical jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic peoples frequently coin many new words drawn from party jargon, mechanical arts, or trade, which tend to serve business, party passions, or public administration rather than elevated thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: be cautious adopting such neologisms; they often mark transient or utilitarian concerns and can erode language in metaphysics and theology. Example: democratic coinages often lack the learned roots of aristocratic neologisms and reflect immediate commercial or political needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve register discrimination between vulgar and refined expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Style rules that distinguish vulgar from refined expressions are weakened in democracies, where people carry terms across ranks and use them without discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: mixing registers so origin of words is lost and style rules are abolished. Recommendation: where appropriate, maintain distinctions rooted in the nature of the things expressed, even if social conventions erode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer specificity over excessive abstraction / generic terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic languages overuse generic and abstract expressions (e.g., 'capacites', 'actualities', 'eventualities'), which enlarge thought but also make it obscure; abstract personifications (e.g., treating 'equality' as an acting agent) render ideas less clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: favor particularizing and concrete expressions when clarity is required. Anti-patterns: habitual use of abstract nouns to allow vagueness or to mask uncertainty; personifying abstractions to avoid specifying referents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use abstraction to conceal uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Because democratic individuals entertain unsettled ideas, they prefer loose expressions and abstractions which permit shifting meanings; this undermines precise thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring note: writing that uses abstraction to hide shaky reasoning or to allow shifting interpretation should be marked down. Prefer phrasing that ties abstract terms to concrete referents when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: When introducing innovations, seek semantic stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The common expedient of giving an unwonted meaning to an existing word is simple and convenient but dangerous; without a permanent tribunal to settle meanings, words can remain ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: ensure new usages are clearly established and not left to conflicting adoptions by successive writers. Anti-pattern: informal semantic drift that produces multiple competing senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of poetry: poetry as search and delineation of the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is the search and the delineation of the ideal: the poet suppresses some of what exists, adds imaginary touches, and combines circumstances to complete and extend nature; verse alone does not constitute poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for producers: aim to present an idealized, adorned vision rather than a mere factual account. Anti-pattern: equating mere versification or plain description with poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select poetic subjects suited to democratic sensibilities (man, future, destiny)
rubrics_metrics.description: In democratic ages the most fruitful sources of poetry are man himself, the destinies of mankind, passions and ideas, and visions of the future rather than past legends, gods, or isolated great persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producer guidance: emphasize humanity as a whole, the future and progress, inner souls and passions. Anti-pattern: relying on antique heroes, legends, or supernatural personifications that no longer resonate with a democratic readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid individual-focused idealization in democratic contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Because individuals in democracies are seen as small and alike, poets cannot typically idealize particular persons; instead they should generalize to include the nation or mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: use general imagery or collective subjects rather than attempting to make a single, ordinary individual the locus of lofty idealization. Scoring note: effectiveness of generalization and ability to evoke the collective ideal matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on descriptive nature poetry in mature democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive poetry of streams and mountains may appear in transitions, but ultimately democracy diverts imaginative attention from external nature to man himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producer guidance: treat nature descriptively only insofar as it illuminates human concerns; avoid making inanimate nature the chief poetic source in fully democratic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer delineation of passions and ideas over persons and achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic poets will prefer to delineate passions and ideas; the inner soul and moral/psychological depths are better material for the ideal than outward dress or fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: works focusing on inner conflict, universal passions, or humanity's destiny score higher than mere accounts of achievements or social status. Anti-pattern: surface-level portraits without exploration of interiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle providential or metaphysical themes implicitly and broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic poetry should avoid literalized gods or demons; instead, it should connect events to broad providential designs without explicit personification of divine agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producer guidance: suggest universal moral or providential patterns through human events and destinies; avoid heavy-handed supernatural personification that seems out of step with democratic skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial or frigid personifications in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Using virtues and vices as frigid personifications is less effective in democratic ages; authenticity requires showing them as features of real human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: allegorical figures used where psychological realism would be more resonant. Prefer concrete humanized depictions of moral qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inflated, pompous diction when attempting poetic style
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who speak plainly in business but attempt poetical diction often become inflated and pompous; democratic writers may expand imaginations to the gigantic, producing overblown imagery and incoherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: lavishing extravagant imagery on ordinary subjects; tendency to create monstrous, exaggerated descriptions. Recommendation: restraint and proportionality in imagery and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proportionality and coherence in poetic imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Because democratic readers demand vast conceptions but lack taste to gauge proportion, authors must self-regulate to avoid producing works that are out of proportion or incoherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring note: evaluate balance between ambition and coherence; penalize works that sacrifice intelligibility for grandiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic writing should prioritize immediacy and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatre reaches spectators without time for reflection or learned preparation; drama therefore should be immediate, striking, and accessible to the unprepared public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producer guidance: craft plays that engage quickly and directly; don't rely on erudition or obscure classical references that a general audience cannot appreciate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage works should reflect present life and a medley of social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies the stage ought to show the medley of conditions, feelings, and opinions present in society rather than a narrow selection of aristocratic personages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: include diverse classes and everyday realities; anti-pattern: theatre that depicts only princes or persons of quality, which signals aristocratic tastes out of step with democratic audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use theatrical reception as a barometer of popular taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Because spectators are swept by immediate impression, the theatre often reveals the people's literary tendencies before they appear elsewhere; playwrights should be mindful that the pit's taste can govern reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: test dramatic work for immediate audience effect; consider how unprepared viewers will respond, since the stage can rapidly indicate or shape broader literary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing aristocratic stylistic rules on democratic drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocratic control of the stage enforces selection of personages and modes of expression; democratic drama should free itself from such imposed modes to better reflect the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: strict adherence to ancient dramatic precedents and elite stylistic constraints when writing for a democratic theatre. Recommendation: adapt style and selection to the democratic public's expectations and experiences.
